Trap findings in this job:
- TSQL-13 lines 61-71: #open_claims temp table becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-01 lines 73-73: status is VARCHAR; IN ('OPEN','REOPENED') matches case variants under CI collation, Spark binary compare drops them.
- TSQL-02 lines 73-73: status VARCHAR values with trailing spaces ('OPEN ') still match in SQL Server, not in Spark.
- TSQL-13 lines 81-86: #reserve temp table becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-01 lines 90-91: PARTITION BY reserve_type (VARCHAR) groups case variants together for the latest-reserve pick; Spark would split them.
- TSQL-02 lines 90-91: PARTITION BY reserve_type ignores trailing spaces in SQL Server; Spark partitions 'EXPENSE ' separately.
- TSQL-13 lines 101-108: #money temp table becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-01 lines 106-106: reserve_type = 'INDEMNITY' on VARCHAR matches 'Indemnity' under CI collation; Spark would not.
- TSQL-02 lines 106-106: reserve_type = 'INDEMNITY' ignores trailing spaces in SQL Server.
- TSQL-01 lines 107-107: reserve_type = 'EXPENSE' on VARCHAR is case-insensitive in legacy.
- TSQL-02 lines 107-107: reserve_type = 'EXPENSE' ignores trailing spaces in SQL Server.
- TSQL-05 lines 136-136: handler_code is nullable; '+' concatenation makes claim_ref NULL when handler_code is NULL; must use concat (not concat_ws).
- TSQL-16 lines 143-143: CONVERT style 103 gives dd/mm/yyyy; Spark needs date_format 'dd/MM/yyyy'.
- TSQL-16 lines 145-145: CONVERT(CHAR(6), d, 112) truncates yyyymmdd to yyyymm; Spark needs date_format 'yyyyMM'.
- TSQL-04 lines 146-146: DATEDIFF(DAY) on DATE equals day difference, but Spark datediff(end,start) reverses argument order; naive translation flips the sign.

Trap cards:
### TSQL-01 (semantic): Case-insensitive collation in =, IN, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, PARTITION BY and joins
Legacy: Under a case-insensitive collation such as SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS, text compares equal regardless of letter case (and of trailing spaces, see TSQL-02): state = 'ACTIVE' also matches 'Active' and 'active'; GROUP BY, DISTINCT, PARTITION BY and join keys put case variants together. The stored value is returned unchanged.
Spark: Spark compares strings in binary order: 'Active' <> 'ACTIVE', so a filter drops case variants, a GROUP BY splits them into separate groups and a join misses them.
Fix: Compare, group, partition and join on upper(rtrim(x)) (or collate(x, 'UTF8_LCASE_RTRIM')) while selecting the original column for output. Never change the stored value unless the legacy code does (e.g. UPPER in the SELECT). Use rtrim, not trim: leading spaces count.
Example: WHERE o.order_state IN ('SHIPPED', 'BILLED') -> F.upper(F.rtrim('order_state')).isin('SHIPPED', 'BILLED')

### TSQL-02 (semantic): Comparisons ignore trailing spaces; CHAR(n) pads with spaces
Legacy: SQL Server pads the shorter string with spaces before comparing, so 'WEST ' = 'WEST' (also in IN, GROUP BY and joins). CHAR(n) and NCHAR(n) values are stored and returned padded to n characters: 'AB' in a CHAR(4) column is 'AB '. LEN() ignores trailing spaces (TSQL-15). Leading spaces always count.
Spark: Spark compares strings exactly, so 'WEST ' <> 'WEST', and its string type never pads. A value read from a CHAR source column keeps whatever spaces it was stored with.
Fix: rtrim both sides of every text comparison, grouping and join key. Where the legacy output column is CHAR(n)/NCHAR(n), pad the value with rpad(x, n, ' ') (NULL stays NULL) so the output matches the stored legacy value. A CHAR(n) source column read into an expression keeps its padding (e.g. in + concatenation).
Example: account_type CHAR(4) ... WHERE region = 'WEST' -> F.rpad('account_type', 4, ' ') ... F.rtrim('region') == 'WEST'

### TSQL-04 (semantic): DATEDIFF counts boundaries crossed, not elapsed periods
Legacy: DATEDIFF(datepart, a, b) counts the datepart boundaries crossed between a and b: DATEDIFF(year, '2025-12-31', '2026-01-01') = 1 and DATEDIFF(month, '2025-01-31', '2025-02-01') = 1. DATEDIFF(week, ...) counts Sundays crossed, whatever SET DATEFIRST says. DATEDIFF(day, ...) on DATE values equals the day difference.
Spark: datediff(end, start) counts days (arguments reversed); months_between returns a fraction with its own month-end rule; floor(months/12) counts elapsed years, not boundaries.
Fix: year: year(b) - year(a). quarter: (year(b)*4 + quarter(b)) - (year(a)*4 + quarter(a)). month: (year(b)*12 + month(b)) - (year(a)*12 + month(a)). week: the difference of Sunday-anchored week numbers, floor(datediff(x, DATE'1899-12-31') / 7) for b minus a. day: datediff(b, a). Mind the argument order: T-SQL is (part, start, end), Spark's datediff is (end, start).
Example: DATEDIFF(YEAR, e.hire_date, @AsOfDate) -> F.year(as_of) - F.year('hire_date')

### TSQL-05 (semantic): + concatenation with NULL yields NULL
Legacy: With CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL ON (the default), 'A' + NULL is NULL, so a whole concatenation is NULL when any part is. CONCAT() and CONCAT_WS() treat NULL as empty.
Spark: Spark's + is arithmetic only; concat() returns NULL when any argument is NULL, while concat_ws() skips NULLs and format_string writes 'null'.
Fix: Translate T-SQL + on strings to F.concat(...) (NULL if any part is NULL). Translate T-SQL CONCAT() to concat of coalesce(x, '') parts, and CONCAT_WS to concat_ws. CHAR(n) parts keep their padding inside the concatenation (TSQL-02).
Example: a.first_name + ' ' + a.middle_name + ' ' + a.last_name -> F.concat('first_name', F.lit(' '), 'middle_name', F.lit(' '), 'last_name')

### TSQL-13 (construct): Temp tables
Legacy: #temp tables hold intermediate results for the session.
Spark: Intermediate results are DataFrames or temporary views.
Fix: Make each #temp table a DataFrame (or temp view). Keep its column types: SELECT INTO creates columns with the source expressions' types, which can matter downstream.
Example: SELECT ... INTO #active_orders FROM dbo.orders -> active_orders = orders.where(...)

### TSQL-16 (semantic): CONVERT style codes
Legacy: CONVERT(type, date, style) formats dates by style: 101 mm/dd/yyyy, 103 dd/mm/yyyy, 104 dd.mm.yyyy, 105 dd-mm-yyyy, 106 dd mon yyyy, 111 yyyy/mm/dd, 112 yyyymmdd, 120 yyyy-mm-dd hh:mi:ss, 121 with milliseconds, 23 yyyy-mm-dd. Converting into a shorter CHAR(n)/VARCHAR(n) silently keeps the first n characters: CONVERT(CHAR(6), d, 112) is yyyymm.
Spark: A cast to string gives yyyy-MM-dd; date_format needs a Java pattern; nothing truncates.
Fix: Use date_format with the style's pattern ('MM/dd/yyyy' for 101, 'dd/MM/yyyy' for 103, 'dd.MM.yyyy' for 104, 'dd-MM-yyyy' for 105, 'yyyy/MM/dd' for 111, 'yyyyMMdd' for 112, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss' for 120, 'yyyy-MM-dd' for 23), then cut to the target length with substring(x, 1, n) where the target type is shorter.
Example: CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), o.order_date, 101), CONVERT(CHAR(8), o.ship_date, 120) -> F.date_format('order_date', 'MM/dd/yyyy'), F.substring(F.date_format('ship_date', 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), 1, 8)

1) Possible legacy bug (row fan-out): #money LEFT JOINs both claim_payments and #reserve on claim_id before GROUP BY (lines 109-115). A claim can have up to two reserve rows (INDEMNITY and EXPENSE), so SUM(p.amount) counts each payment once per reserve row, and total_paid and incurred can come out doubled. The migration must reproduce this behaviour to match the legacy output; n_payments is not affected because it uses COUNT(DISTINCT). 2) claim_ref is NULL whenever handler_code is NULL, because string concatenation with + returns NULL by default (CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL). 3) policy_number comes from the single latest snapshot_date on or before @AsOfDate across the whole table, picked into the variable @snapshot_date (lines 121-123). If a policy is missing from that snapshot, policy_number is NULL; the job does not fall back to an earlier snapshot. 4) Reserve types other than INDEMNITY or EXPENSE are dropped, and the reserve_date filter only changes the reserve values, not which claim rows appear. 5) The PARTITION BY claim_id, reserve_type in the reserve ROW_NUMBER is listed as a ranks edge with lower confidence (0.6). 6) The joins to #money and #reserve keep every open claim, so the output has one row per claim from stg.claims that passes the filters on lines 73-74.

structured_output.code:
"""T04 usp_build_claims_summary: migrated from estate/tsql/T04_usp_build_claims_summary.sql.

Legacy SHA-256: 632841c99f0c5919975c6fd2266ab04b33e1ba87424c55bbfbe7b0223f3bc975
Written by: LANSH translator (Claude)
Traps handled: TSQL-01, TSQL-02, TSQL-04, TSQL-05, TSQL-13, TSQL-16
Bugs reproduced on purpose (# LANSH-DEFECT): payment/reserve join fan-out inflates total_paid and incurred
"""
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession, Window
import pyspark.sql.functions as F


def run(spark: SparkSession, inputs: dict[str, DataFrame], params: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, DataFrame]:
    claims = inputs["stg.claims"]
    payments = inputs["stg.claim_payments"]
    reserves = inputs["stg.claim_reserves"]
    snapshots = inputs["stg.policy_snapshots"]

    as_of = F.to_date(F.lit(params["AsOfDate"]))

    # TSQL-13: #open_claims -> DataFrame (lines 63-74)
    # TSQL-01 / TSQL-02: status IN (...) ignores case and trailing spaces under the CI collation
    open_claims = (
        claims
        .where(
            F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("status"))).isin("OPEN", "REOPENED")
            & (F.col("reported_date") <= as_of)
        )
        .select(
            F.col("claim_id"),
            F.col("claim_number"),
            F.col("policy_id"),
            F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("lob_code"))).alias("lob_code"),
            F.col("status"),
            F.col("handler_code"),
            F.col("loss_date"),
            F.col("reported_date"),
        )
    )

    oc_ids = open_claims.select("claim_id")

    # TSQL-13: #reserve -> DataFrame (lines 83-95)
    # TSQL-01 / TSQL-02: PARTITION BY reserve_type puts case / trailing-space variants together
    w_res = (
        Window.partitionBy(F.col("claim_id"), F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("reserve_type"))))
        .orderBy(F.col("reserve_date").desc(), F.col("reserve_id").desc(), F.col("_row_seq").asc())
    )
    reserve = (
        reserves
        .where(F.col("reserve_date") <= as_of)
        .join(oc_ids, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w_res))
        .where(F.col("rn") == 1)
        .select("claim_id", "reserve_type", "reserve_amount")
    )

    # TSQL-13: #money -> DataFrame (lines 103-115)
    pay = (
        payments
        .where(F.col("payment_date") <= as_of)
        .select(F.col("claim_id").alias("p_claim_id"), F.col("payment_id"), F.col("amount"))
    )
    rsv = reserve.select(
        F.col("claim_id").alias("r_claim_id"), F.col("reserve_type"), F.col("reserve_amount")
    )
    rtype = F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("reserve_type")))  # TSQL-01 / TSQL-02 on lines 106-107
    money = (
        oc_ids
        .join(pay, F.col("claim_id") == F.col("p_claim_id"), "left")
        .join(rsv, F.col("claim_id") == F.col("r_claim_id"), "left")  # LANSH-DEFECT: payments x reserve rows fan-out before GROUP BY
        .groupBy("claim_id")
        .agg(
            F.countDistinct(F.col("payment_id")).alias("n_payments"),
            F.coalesce(F.sum(F.col("amount")), F.lit(0)).alias("total_paid"),  # LANSH-DEFECT: SUM counts each payment once per reserve row
            F.coalesce(
                F.max(F.when(rtype == "INDEMNITY", F.col("reserve_amount"))), F.lit(0)
            ).alias("indemnity_reserve"),
            F.coalesce(
                F.max(F.when(rtype == "EXPENSE", F.col("reserve_amount"))), F.lit(0)
            ).alias("expense_reserve"),
        )
    )

    # @snapshot_date = MAX(snapshot_date) <= @AsOfDate (lines 121-123); NULL matches nothing
    snap = (
        snapshots
        .where(F.col("snapshot_date") <= as_of)
        .agg(F.max(F.col("snapshot_date")).alias("snap_date"))
    )
    ps = (
        snapshots
        .join(snap, F.col("snapshot_date") == F.col("snap_date"), "inner")
        .select(F.col("policy_id").alias("ps_policy_id"), F.col("policy_number"))
    )

    joined = (
        open_claims
        .join(money, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .join(ps, F.col("policy_id") == F.col("ps_policy_id"), "left")
    )

    result = joined.select(
        F.col("claim_id"),
        F.col("claim_number"),
        # TSQL-05: '+' concatenation is NULL if any part (e.g. handler_code) is NULL
        F.concat(
            F.col("lob_code"), F.lit("/"), F.col("claim_number"), F.lit("/"), F.col("handler_code")
        ).alias("claim_ref"),
        F.col("policy_id"),
        F.col("policy_number"),
        F.col("lob_code"),
        F.col("status"),
        F.col("handler_code"),
        F.col("loss_date"),
        # TSQL-16: CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), d, 103) -> dd/MM/yyyy
        F.date_format(F.col("loss_date"), "dd/MM/yyyy").alias("loss_date_text"),
        F.col("reported_date"),
        # TSQL-16: CONVERT(CHAR(6), d, 112) -> first 6 chars of yyyyMMdd; TSQL-02 CHAR(6) padding
        F.rpad(
            F.substring(F.date_format(F.col("reported_date"), "yyyyMMdd"), 1, 6), 6, " "
        ).alias("reported_period"),
        # TSQL-04: DATEDIFF(DAY, start, end) -> datediff(end, start)
        F.datediff(as_of, F.col("reported_date")).alias("days_open"),
        F.col("n_payments"),
        F.col("total_paid"),
        F.col("indemnity_reserve"),
        F.col("expense_reserve"),
        (F.col("indemnity_reserve") + F.col("expense_reserve")).alias("current_reserve"),
        (F.col("total_paid") + F.col("indemnity_reserve") + F.col("expense_reserve")).alias("incurred"),  # LANSH-DEFECT: incurred carries the fanned-out total_paid
        as_of.alias("as_of_date"),
    )

    return {"rpt.claims_summary": result}

defects.intended: Total paid to date should count each payment once: work out payments and reserves separately per claim (or pre-aggregate them) before joining.
defects.title: Payment/reserve join fan-out inflates total_paid and incurred
defects.what_it_does: #money LEFT JOINs claim_payments and #reserve on claim_id before GROUP BY. Each payment row is repeated once for every reserve row the claim has in #reserve (one per distinct reserve type, other types such as non-INDEMNITY/EXPENSE included). So SUM(p.amount) gives paid multiplied by the number of reserve rows (when there are 2 or more), and incurred carries the same inflated figure. n_payments (COUNT DISTINCT) and the MAX reserves are not affected.

structured_output.notes: 1) The fan-out is reproduced by copying the join shape exactly: open claims LEFT JOIN payments (payment_date <= AsOfDate, filtered before the left join, which gives the same result) LEFT JOIN #reserve, then GROUP BY claim_id. #reserve keeps every reserve type, not just INDEMNITY and EXPENSE, so other types also multiply the payment rows, just as in legacy. 2) The latest reserve per (claim_id, reserve_type) is picked with the type key upper(rtrim()), so case and trailing-space variants share one partition. The stored reserve_type is kept, and the INDEMNITY/EXPENSE CASE checks also use upper(rtrim()). Ties are broken by _row_seq ascending after reserve_date DESC, reserve_id DESC; DESC puts NULLs last, as in SQL Server. 3) @snapshot_date is the single latest snapshot_date <= AsOfDate across the whole table. If there is none, the equality join matches nothing and policy_number is NULL. A policy missing from that snapshot also gets NULL, with no fallback to an earlier snapshot, matching legacy. 4) n_payments comes from countDistinct (bigint) and the harness casts it to INT. The money columns stay exact decimals until the harness casts them to decimal(14,2). 5) claim_ref uses F.concat, so it is NULL when handler_code (or any other part) is NULL. 6) If stg.claims has duplicate claim_ids, the joins repeat them just as legacy does; legacy would then fail on the primary key.
